name: Statue of John Hope, 4th Earl of Hopetoun
address: Forecourt of Dundas House, 36 St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2YB
description: A life-size bronze of John Hope, 4th Earl of Hopetoun (1765-1823), the general who took command of the British army at Corunna after Sir John Moore was killed. Sculpted by Thomas Campbell, it stands in the railed forecourt of Dundas House, long the head office of the Royal Bank of Scotland. Hope wears a Roman toga rather than uniform and stands beside a horse with its head bowed - a pedestrian figure, not a mounted one. A stepped granite plinth carries a drum-ended bronze pedestal, its inscription written by Sir Walter Scott.
interesting_fact: It was never meant to be here. Edinburgh commissioned the statue in 1824 for Charlotte Square, then judged it unsuitable; it went unplaced for years until the bank accepted it in 1834 and set it in its own forecourt. The accidental siting produced the square's best in-joke: the Earl stands looking west across the gardens directly at the Melville Monument and Henry Dundas - who was his brother-in-law, having married the Earl's sister Lady Jane Hope in 1793. In 2020 the statue was drawn into Edinburgh's review of monuments with slavery links, over Hope's part in crushing Fedon's rebellion in Grenada in 1795-96.

name: Lion of Scotland
description: A 20-tonne recumbent lion hand-carved from a single boulder of pink granite by sculptor Ronald Rae, moved here in 2010. The stone is Corrennie granite from Aberdeenshire and the finished animal runs to roughly 17 feet long and 8 feet high. It was first sited in Holyrood Park, on the ground between the Palace of Holyroodhouse and the new Scottish Parliament, placed there deliberately beneath Arthur's Seat - a hill long read as a lion in its own right.
interesting_fact: It's been voted Edinburgh's best-loved sculpture - and took over a year to carve using hand tools only, with no power tools at any stage. When the Holyrood loan was due to expire in 2008, Scottish Blue Badge guides raised a petition and thousands of residents and visitors signed it; that won a two-year reprieve, and on 25 April 2010 the lion made the mile-long journey across town to St Andrew Square Garden. It came on loan rather than by purchase, financed by Essential Edinburgh and private sponsors, and Rae has said he hopes the city will one day buy it outright. Technically, it is still a visitor.

name: Melville Monument
description: A fluted Doric column over 45 metres tall, inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome and topped with a statue of Henry Dundas, 1st Viscount Melville. Built 1821-27 and weighing around 1,500 tons, the monument was engineered with help from Robert Stevenson - the lighthouse-building grandfather of novelist Robert Louis Stevenson, brought in because nothing this large had been attempted in Scotland before. The design was William Burn's, and the roughly 15-foot figure on top was carved by Robert Forrest to a model by Sir Francis Chantrey.
interesting_fact: Dundas was so politically powerful in late-18th-century Scotland he was nicknamed 'The Uncrowned King of Scotland' - and this monument is literally the 'big man in the sky' the game's own clue points players toward. In 1806 he became the last person ever impeached in the UK, for misappropriating public funds; a plaque added to the monument in 2021 also addresses his role in delaying the abolition of the slave trade. The £8,000 bill was met by subscription from the officers and men of the Royal Navy, which Dundas had run as First Lord of the Admiralty from 1804.

name: National Portrait Gallery
description: Scotland's national portrait collection, housed in a red sandstone Gothic Revival pile on the north side of Queen Street. Robert Rowand Anderson designed it; it was built 1885-90 and opened in 1889, the stone quarried at Corsehill near Annan in Dumfriesshire. Four octagonal corner turrets with crocketed pinnacles frame a facade studded with niche statues of famous Scots. It was built as a double building - the portrait gallery in the east wing, the National Museum of Antiquities in the west - sharing one Great Hall as a common entrance.
interesting_fact: Nobody was supposed to know who paid for it. In 1882 an anonymous 10,000 pound gift arrived to "set on foot" a national portrait gallery; the donor quietly kept paying until the bill reached roughly 70,000 pounds, and his identity was revealed only on opening day in 1889 - John Ritchie Findlay, proprietor of The Scotsman. It was the first building in the world purpose-built as a portrait gallery. Inside, the Great Hall's arcaded balcony carries William Hole's processional frieze of 155 Scots running backwards in time from Thomas Carlyle to the Stone Age, beneath a ceiling of over 2,000 gold stars.

name: James Clerk Maxwell statue
address: Central reservation, east end of George Street at St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2LL
description: A seated bronze of the physicist James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) by Alexander Stoddart, unveiled 25 November 2008 on the central reservation at the east end of George Street, facing west. Maxwell is shown in Victorian dress at roughly the age he died, holding the spinning colour top he used to investigate colour vision, with his terrier Toby at his feet. Bronze reliefs on the granite plinth show Newton with his prism and Einstein with a warped-spacetime sheet, and a plaque carries Maxwell's equations.

His 1865 formulation ran to twenty equations in twenty variables; the compact vector form the world now calls "Maxwell's equations" was boiled down by Oliver Heaviside two decades later, after Maxwell was dead. The site is apt for a second reason: the Royal Society of Edinburgh, which commissioned the statue and sits a block west, first published Maxwell at fourteen - his 1846 paper on oval curves had to be read aloud to the Society by Professor James Forbes, because a boy that age could not present it himself.

name: Thistle Court
description: Two pairs of modest semi-detached houses facing each other across a small grass court, built in 1767 - the oldest surviving buildings in the whole New Town. They are plain two-storey-and-attic classical houses of sandstone rubble, some of it red, with ashlar dressings: no columns, no pediment, nothing whatsoever to announce that Edinburgh's grandest building project started here. All four are now Category A listed, and the court is thought to have been called Rose Court originally.
interesting_fact: They exist because developer John Young simply ignored James Craig's rigid grid plan and built houses facing each other instead of a terraced row - possibly the oldest semi-detached houses in Scotland. The town council had dangled a £20 premium for the first builder to break ground in the New Town, and Young collected it. The rest of Thistle Street took another twenty-odd years to fill up, put up as plain craft workers' dwellings and workshops - the cheap seats directly behind George Street's mansions - and Craig named it for Scotland's emblem to pair with Rose Street, named for England's.

name: The Dome
description: Built around 1847 to a design by architect David Rhind in the Graeco-Roman style, on the site of the former Physicians' Hall. Its hexastyle Corinthian portico is 95 feet wide with six 35-foot columns, topped by a sculpted pediment by Alexander Handyside Ritchie. Now a Category A listed building, it takes its name from the large glass dome lighting the banking hall inside. Ritchie's pediment group is Fruitfulness attended by Trade and Navigation - the same group the Commercial Bank engraved on its own banknotes, so Scots carried this building around in their pockets.
interesting_fact: The bank that built this grand headquarters eventually merged into the very same Royal Bank of Scotland whose own head office - Dundas House - is the first stop on this walk: once a rival across town, now part of the same institution. The Physicians' Hall it replaced was designed by James Craig, who planned the New Town; its foundation stone was laid in 1776, and when it came down in January 1844 the workmen opened that stone and found silver medals sealed inside.

name: St Andrew's and St George's West Church
description: Built in 1784 as St Andrew's Church - the first church built in the New Town. The design was won in competition by Captain Andrew Frazer of the Royal Engineers, then chief army engineer for Scotland, working with Robert Kay, and its oval interior was the first elliptical church plan in Britain - partly a virtue made of necessity, since the leftover plot was too shallow for a conventional nave. The ceiling was lifted from Robert Wood's 'Ruins of Palmyra' of 1753, with Scottish thistles worked in. The 51-metre steeple was an afterthought, added in 1787.
interesting_fact: The site was originally earmarked for Dundas House (now the RBS HQ landmark) before it was swapped for the church - Sir Lawrence Dundas quietly bought up the square's east side before Craig's plan could be enforced, and the church was bumped along George Street instead. The steeple holds eight bells cast in 1788 at London's Whitechapel foundry, the oldest complete ring in Scotland. And on 18 May 1843 this was the room where the Disruption happened: around a third of the ministers at the General Assembly walked out and founded the Free Church of Scotland.

name: Caledonian Insurance Building
description: A grand former insurance office designed by David Bryce, 1839-40, remodelling one of the plain 1780s townhouses that originally filled this side of George Street. It was worked over again in 1879-80, and the Caledonian finally moved out in 1939, selling the premises to the George Hotel next door; the military promptly requisitioned them for the rest of the war. A man named Forrest Alexander had a £600 fire claim thrown out by his English insurers because his renewal ran one day late, so he set about starting a Scottish one instead. The painter Sir Henry Raeburn sat on the board and designed the company's policy heading, which stayed in use until 1838.

name: Royal Society of Edinburgh
description: Home of Scotland's National Academy of Science and Letters since 1908/09 - a Category A building with a distinctive green cupola. The present block went up in 1908-09 to a design by J M Dick Peddie, faced in fossil-bearing Portland stone from Dorset over a base course of Creetown granite: paler, harder and glossier than the local sandstone on either side of it, which is why the frontage reads slightly cold next to its neighbours. Adam Smith, Joseph Black and James Hutton all sat on the first Council, and it was to this Society that Hutton read his 'Theory of the Earth', the paper that effectively invented deep geological time. name: Susan Ferrier's Home
description: Home of novelist Susan Ferrier from 1784 to around 1830. She was two years old when the family moved in - the house was numbered 11 at the time - and she stayed for most of her adult life, writing all three of her novels under this roof. Her father James Ferrier was a Writer to the Signet and a Principal Clerk of the Court of Session, which put him at the next desk to Walter Scott and gave his daughter a standing invitation into Edinburgh's literary establishment. Today, this specific townhouse has been absorbed into the historic, luxury hotel InterContinental Edinburgh The George.
interesting_fact: Sometimes called 'the Scottish Jane Austen', Ferrier was a contemporary and friend of Sir Walter Scott. All three of her novels appeared anonymously and she was not publicly named as their author until 1851, three years before her death. The fees tell you how well they sold: Blackwood paid £150 for 'Marriage' in 1818, and by 'Destiny' in 1831 Robert Cadell was handing over £1,700, a small fortune for a novel then. Scott rated her company as much as her books, calling her conversation 'the least exigeant of any author, female at least'. Failing eyesight made her a recluse; she is buried at St Cuthbert's.

name: The Assembly Rooms
description: Opened 1787, the most important surviving building of its type in the UK - Category A listed, still an events venue today. It was designed by John Henderson, who won the competition for it in 1781 and then died in February 1786 before it was finished, and paid for by public subscription at a cost of over £6,000 on a site the town council handed over for nothing. The opening event, on 11 January 1787, was the Caledonian Hunt Ball. The great portico came later, in 1818, and the Music Hall behind it in 1843.

Dickens and Thackeray both read here afterwards, and since 1981 it has been one of the big Fringe venues.

name: Pink Sandstone Among Yellow Free-Stone
description: Former Dowells Auctioneers, built 1907-08 - the one building on this stretch built in pale pink sandstone rather than the local yellow/cream sandstone everyone else used. The architects were John Nichol Scott and Alexander Lorne Campbell, and behind the front block sit two plain top-lit auction rooms, the eastern one of real historic interest. Dowell's ran sales here for generations; its catalogues and roup rolls, from 1879 onwards, are now held by the National Library of Scotland.
interesting_fact: The pink is New Red Sandstone from Locharbriggs near Dumfries, and it is here for a reason. Most of the New Town was built from Craigleith quarry on the city's own north-western edge, but by the Edwardian period the railways had made Dumfriesshire stone cheap to haul seventy miles north, and red stone was fashionable besides. So the odd one out is not just a different colour - it is a different rock entirely, laid down in a Permian desert something like eighty million years after the swampy Carboniferous sands that make up its neighbours. Craigleith worked from 1615 and did not close until 1942.

name: Hidden Back-Lane White Tiles
description: White glazed brick tiling lining a New Town back lane - a common Georgian/Victorian trick to bounce light down narrow service lanes with no direct sun. The lanes themselves are pure Craig: every one of his blocks is cut through by a mews lane, lined with stables and coach houses so carriages never appeared at the front door. Rose Street North Lane served the discreet back entrances of the Princes Street houses. Well into the 19th century some also held byres for the cows that supplied the surrounding households with milk.
interesting_fact: Confirmed on-site with a real photo - white glazed brick pillars between the windows, plus a decorative black-and-white diamond-pattern tile band lower down. Glazed brick like this was mass-produced from the 1860s onwards by fireclay firms like Burmantofts of Leeds, and sunless spaces such as lightwells were routinely lined with it to reflect daylight deeper in. It had a second use in a coal-smoke city that called itself Auld Reekie - a glazed face sheds soot and can be sluiced clean with a bucket, which is also why it lined the stables and dairies these lanes held.
